## [2026-06-09T12:14:34Z] assistant_thought (afterAgentThought)

The `assignSeats` line fails to compile because of the `setup_election_sim_only` condition.

Dendry might be misreading `setup_election_sim_only` as a goto label because of the word `setup` at the start of the quality name. The original condition with `=` assignment still compiles fine.

A shorter flag like `Q.election_sim_boot` could avoid the parsing issue. Alternatively, `assignSeats` might not need a guard at all. The election simulation scene sets `Q.setup_goto_main = 0` but leaves `economic_assets_bootstrap_return` unset, so `assignSeats` likely does not run during normal menu entry anyway.

The original condition assigns 2 to `bootstrap_return` and relies on the truthiness of that assignment to trigger `assignSeats`. This means `assignSeats` fires unconditionally whenever the function exists, since the assignment itself evaluates as truthy.

The assignment in the condition always yields truthy, so `assignSeats` cannot be skipped by setting `bootstrap_return` to zero. A dedicated flag like `Q.election_sim_skip_assign_seats` will be set in `election_simulation` on arrival. `setup_functions` will then use a standalone semicolon-separated check instead of an `&&` expression.

The proposed fix uses a standalone `if` block with braces for the skip flag, followed by an `else if` that keeps the original `bootstrap_return` assignment and `typeof` check for `assignSeatsFromInitialPolling`.

 return PP_DISTRICT_MAJORITY\n}\n\nfunction ppSeatsForChamber(chamberId, districtId, opts) {\n    opts = opts || {}\n    if (opts.availableSeats) { return ppCloneSeats(opts.availableSeats) }\n    if ## [2026-06-09T12:31:37Z] assistant (afterAgentResponse)

You were right — `{! Q.election_sim_coalitions_Docks !}` doesn’t insert HTML in Dendry. It treats the inside as a JS expression, so you get the literal `Q.…` text instead of rendered markup.

Fixed using the same pattern as Stacy’s paramilitary report and Jacobs’ holdings:

1. **Placeholder divs** in the scene: `{!<div class="election-sim-coalition-slot" data-coalition-target="Vats"></div>!}`
2. **`on-display`** on `@show_results` calls `Q.renderElectionSimCoalitionReports()`
3. **`renderElectionSimCoalitionReports()`** in `political_power_runtime` fills those divs with the HTML built by `refreshElectionSimCoalitionReports()`

After `npm run make-html`, reload the election sim — you should see the status line and bullet list under executive and each district.

`setup_functions` still contains a `!` operator. This likely explains why the election seats reverted to zero.

The `!` inside `!==` may terminate the block. `!Q.electionV2` is another bad spot. The fix is to replace `!` with `== null` or `== 0`.

The bootstrap check now uses `typeof` to detect functions, then sets a flag. `show_results` will default `year` to 2300 and `month` to 1 when they are null or zero.

`update_projections` now runs with `allDistricts: true` when the function exists. `refreshElectionSimCoalitionReports` and `renderElectionSimCoalitionReports` are guarded by `typeof` checks. The `@refresh` trigger also calls `update_projections` before refreshing reports.

The `if (!Q.year)` guard in `show_results` is the main culprit. It breaks the block before `update_projections` can run. When the APIs already exist on the first year, bootstrap is skipped entirely. The user lands directly in `show_results`, so `update_projections` never executes and the seat counts stay at zero.

Three paths were considered. In every case, the seat counts should already be populated. The zero seats suggest the election runtime never completed its bootstrap even though the APIs appear present. The root cause may be that `political_power` loaded earlier, causing the election simulation to skip bootstrap entirely.

On a first visit, the bootstrap block itself may break at the `!==` operator. Dendry could stop parsing entirely at the `!` character, leaving `Q.update_projections` undefined. If the bootstrap never executes, `Proj_*` variables are never initialized, so the seat counts remain zero.

The root bootstrap and `show_results` both break at their `!` operators. `election_sim_setup_jump` never becomes 1, so the scene never jumps. `show_results` halts at `!Q.year` before `update_projections` can run. This leaves every `Proj_*` variable at zero. Users who enter the election simulator directly without starting the full game hit both failures. Those who start the full game first should already have the APIs loaded.

The `@refresh` block also needs fixing with strict equality. The `POLITICAL_POWER_API` definition should include `renderElectionSimCoalitionReports` so the election simulator can find it.

The API list is missing `renderElectionSimCoalitionReports`. The root bootstrap checks for both `update_projections` and `refreshElectionSimCoalitionReports`. A partial `political_power` load would leave the simulator without the needed APIs. The fix targets `election_simulation.scene.dry` and rebuilds. The root condition could be simplified to rely only on the election and political power APIs.

## [2026-06-09T12:39:38Z] assistant (afterAgentResponse)

The zero seats were a Dendry parsing issue, not the coalition HTML change.

In `{! !}` blocks, a bare `!` ends the block early. `@show_results` had:

```javascript
if (!Q.year) { Q.year = 2300 }
```

Dendry stopped there, so `Q.update_projections({ allDistricts: true })` never ran and every `Proj_*` stayed at its default 0. The root bootstrap check had the same problem with `!==`.

**Fix:** Rewrote those checks to avoid leading `!` / `!==` — e.g. `Q.year == null || Q.year == 0` and positive `typeof … == 'function'` tests. Also call `renderElectionSimCoalitionReports()` from `on-arrival` on show/refresh so coalition lists paint even if `on-display` timing is odd.

Rebuilt with `npm run make-html`. Opening Election simulation from the menu should show non-zero projections again (e.g. executive D ~38, Vats C ~11 at default state). Refresh should work too.

If anything still looks wrong after a hard reload, say what you see and we can trace further.

The player could also voluntarily negotiate for control (not sure how this will be triggered).\n\nThe leverage loop is heavily influenced by the fact that trading away toleration is the easiest way to get leverage.  The major phases will result in some political shifts but mostly in order to have control somewhere you need to tolerate somewhere else.  Increasing vote share increases how much leverage you can get by trading away toleration and reduces how much leverage you need to secure support for your own governments.\n\nThe Hate groups wont ever support you because they are modeled on the Nazi strategy of refusing to accept a minority role in someone elses coalition while planning the violent siezure of power.  So keeping their vote share down is important because any seats they hold are unavailable for making deals.\n\nI'm not covering any possibilities besides toleration, control and anarchy because I'm afraid of scope creep.  I'm going to assume that generally the corps and gangs are at each other's throats so much that the player can always negotiate a toleration agreement with them.  If the corporations or gangs are more afraid of the player then of each other then you will be rapidly arriving at the endgame where they go to war with you.\n\nCovering the loss of control in Aurora is something I think can be left for later.\n\nbandwidth is per group.  If you need the support from the 7 families, you can't use leverage with the Sharks to get that support.\n\nThe reforms shrink the bandwidth because they raise reprisal.  Bandwidth is just the term I was using for the gap between leverage and reprisal.\n\nAt the grace year expiration, the player would need to immediately negotiate for control of the government or the corporations will agree on putting a \"neutral\" corporate flunky in charge, this is the same figure who was in charge before the tether snap incident.\n\nVoluntarily negotiating for control is about getting leverage by going to toleration or swapping support because you need to free up leverage with a group.\n\nIf Aurora toleration is implemented it should be something of a move of desperation, a corporation or syndicate in control of Aurora will do tons of damage at a very fast pace.\n\n## Aurora at game start\n\nTreat Aurora as **partly reformed**: the democrats already hold the council and some reforms are baked in.  The player does not need to negotiate control there initially, but can enact additional reforms from day one.  Each new reform still spikes reprisal (and needs a post-reform bandwidth check if we apply that rule uniformly), though reprisal magnitudes should be **lower than corporate-district equivalents** — tuning TBD per reform card.  Losing Aurora later remains out of scope for v1; holding it while reprisal accumulates is the early-game pressure.\n\n## Witness protection (anti-crime reform, TBD)\n\nSingle track: **`witness_protection_level`** (0 = none). Each step below bumps the level; higher = larger, more capable program. Aurora-first; good fit for partly-reformed district.\n\n| Level bump | How | Reprisal |\n|------------|-----|----------|\n| 0 → 1 | Aurora council reform — establish pilot program | Small, **gangs** |\n| +1 | Aurora council reform — grow local capacity | More gang reprisal |\n| +1 | Geopolitical deal — joint network with other **cycler waystations** (peer media etc., TBD) | **None** (secret) |\n| per district | Other districts **join** program (unlock when level ≥ 2) | Bargain — low reprisal, strong anti-crime |\n\n**District join** unlocks at **level ≥ 2** (established + at least one growth step). Joining a district is cheap reprisal for solid `crime_relief_*` / paramilitary impact (hooks TBD).\n\n**Blind-eye payoff** — Level gates whether the **station manager survives** if the player breaks the blind-eye promise ([`cable_syndicate_blind_eye.scene.dry`](source/scenes/events/cable_syndicate_blind_eye.scene.dry)); replaces today's `police_reform` / `police_investigated` check for Marcus Hale. Threshold TBD (likely level ≥ 2).\n\nState: `witness_protection_level`; optional per-district `witness_protection_join_*` (or fold joins into level / district flags when implementing).\n\n## Pro-democratic dual path (general rule)\n\nBefore a pro-democratic reform vote, two distinct majority coalitions must exist:\n\n- Both reach majority on seat math; the player only **uses one** to pass the bill.\n- Non-D members must be **disjoint** between the two paths (D may appear in both).\n- **H** is excluded from both paths.\n- Any **home-district IG** (corp or syndicate) is excluded from both paths — they will not vote for pro-democratic reforms in their home territory. If multiple IGs call a district home (e.g. Pitts), **none** of them vote for reforms there.\n- Pre-vote: both paths must be affordable (bandwidth to buy non-D support). Post-vote: separate maintenance check after the reprisal spike — the preview paths need not still work afterward.\n- Edge case: a home corp/syndicate may still **prop up the government** after the reform if leverage is high enough (they protect their investment), even though they never voted for the reform. Vote coalition ≠ maintenance coalition.\n\n## Attitude vs affordability\n\n`wary` or `contempt` attitude does **not** block buying support — it usually means `leverage − reprisal` is too small to afford the bandwidth cost. Grey out options on bandwidth, not attitude label.\n\n## Toleration headcount\n\nWhen offering toleration to a home corp that lost its outright majority, **Dem seats count** toward the bloc keeping that leadership in power (e.g. 6C + 4D reaches 10).\n\n## Achievements (add later)\n\n| Title | Icon | Unlock |\n|-------|------|--------|\n| Got 'em by the short hairs. | clothespin | After a pro-democratic reform, a **corporation** supports your government in the post-reform maintenance check without having been in the reform vote coalition. |\n| An offer they can't refuse. | cottonball | Same, but a **syndicate**. |\n\n## Implementation\n\nDraft control-check API (not wired into boot/tick yet): `source/scenes/political_power_runtime.scene.dry` — `Q.ppCheckDistrictControl`, `Q.ppCheckExecutiveControl`, `Q.ppFindProDemocraticDualPaths`, `Q.ppCheckPostReformMaintenance`, etc."

**間** fits well here — it’s the interval or workable space *between* leverage and reprisal, not leverage itself. Same idea as the aesthetic “ma” (negative space, room to act). In game terms: per-IG `leverage − reprisal − committed`; reforms eat into it by raising reprisal.

The Deeps is a special case where it's about winning the trust of the Deepers (something to tackle later)\n3. The Pitts and the Docks are a bit strange so the player might have lots of support there or none at all.  But even there the player will mostly want to leverage point 4.  The Docks differs again in failure mode: if nobody can govern, a corporate flunky retakes the district (same class of fallback as city executive), not anarchy.\n4. The real important dynamic is in the corporate districts and the citywide government.  Here it's all about securing leverage by making sure nobody else has a clean majority, letting you trade away toleration agreements for leverage.\n\n\nIn the corporate home districts the corporations have a huge advantage because of the drones vote.  But if the drones start abstaining en masse and no longer constitute a majority of voters the vote shifts to the 1/2/3rd waves and coops, much less corporation friendly demographics.  \n\nIf a coorporation is knocked out of a majority in it's home district and the player has enough seats to give them a majority, they will be given the option to offer toleration to current district leadership.  This results in a big chunk of leverage on the corporation which lasts as long as the player is keeping them in power.  Losing control of their home district government should be a big blow to the corps.  \n\nWith the city government, the player gets a free year of control after the tether snap event but after that they can continue to control the government if they have enough leverage on corps/syndicates to buy a majority.  If they dont, a corporate flunky is put back in charge.  The player could also negotiate toleration like with district governments.\n\nTo control a district government (without winning an outright majority), the player will need to have leverage to cash in with corporations and syndicates.  The player needs to maintain a leverage over reprisal surplus of a certain size to afford support for control of a district or the city.  If the player can no longer afford the support they will lose the government (unless they can negotiate a new agreement.)  The leverage needs to be paid for every group whose support you needs and scales by how big a share of the seats they have.\n\nWith control of the government of a district or the city, the player can start implementing pro-worker, pro-democratic and anti-crime reforms.  Passing a reform will usually raise the reprisal of syndicates and/or corporations so you need to have excess support sufficient to maintain your government after the reprisal from the reform.  If you can't maintain the government afterwards you can't get the reform implemented.\n\nPro-worker reforms will shift money from the corporation to the voters living in the corporation's home district and the docks.  This will weaken the corporation as well as give reprisal.  The other corps will also gain reprisal unless they are at war with the target.\n\nAnti-crime reforms likewise weaken the syndicates and give reprisal but unlike the corporations the syndicates mostly dont have a stranglehold on a district government.  If you have corporate toleration without dependence on the gangs the corporations wont gain reprisal for you doing anti-crime stuff.\n\nPro-democratic reforms are only possible if the player has enough support to secure a majority both of these ways:\n1) Support from gangs (and independents) without any corporation (or hate) support needed\n2) Support from corporations who dont have the district as their home district (plus independents) without any gang (or hate) support needed.\nSupport for both of these needs to be high enough before the vote.  Additionally you need support high enough to maintain control of the government after the vote (possibly by making a big concession like giving up a government control elsewhere).  Pro democratic reforms will change the electorate (like freeing the drones to vote as they please) and will cause a big reprisal jump for all the gangs and corps.  However if you can maintain control of the government until the next election, suddenly you might find yourself much less depedent on negotiating for support.\n\nBesides these big reforms, just bare control of the government would allow for some smaller stuff like improving the judiciary which wont cause reprisal spikes.  Additionally control of the government would make efforts to improve the police/militia become more effective.\n\nIf the player can't control the government and no corporation has enough votes to control a district government even with toleration from the player, there will instead be an anarchy situation where the corporations and gangs start bribing the district politicians left right and center.  This will be very bad for a home district corporation and very good for the syndicates.  If enough governments collapse this way the gangs might become the main threat not the corporations.  **Exception: the Docks** — like citywide government, the fallback is a **corporate flunky from before** (pre-tether default leadership), not anarchy. District anarchy applies only to the other districts.\n\nThe first step to this is implement a function that checks what, if any coalitions are possible for the player in that district.  This gets checked every time the district votes, allowing the player to negotiate for control if they have the leverage.  If a coalition is possible but the leverage isn't there, it will appear greyed out.  The player can use the district scene to negotiate for a new coalition at any time, including if they weren't previously controlling the government.\n\nsecuring control with leverage would not lower the leverage but it would add **詰** (*tsuma*) — how much of your **間** with that group is packed into ongoing commitments.  **間** (*ma*) is the workable gap `leverage − reprisal`; **詰** is the slice of that gap already spoken for.  So if their attitude is transactional and you lock 3 points of 間 into their support, their attitude stays transactional — you just can't spend that slice elsewhere — and you keep paying that 詰 as long as their support holds up your government.  If you voluntarily give up the government or can no longer afford it, that 詰 clears and the 間 is free again.\n\nCalendar: district control will always be updated after a district election or after the player can't afford the government.  The player can also use the district menu to update this sooner.\n\nThe free year after tether snap is for control of the city government.  The corporations need to leave you in government at least that long to placate the non-Mikasa corporations.  Even if reprisal exceeds leverage they will leave you in place for the one year grace period.  After that yearlong grace period you'll need to negotiate for control again.  You are forced to renegotiate for control if you no longer have enough 間 to control the government.  The player could also voluntarily negotiate for control (not sure how this will be triggered).\n\nThe leverage loop is heavily influenced by the fact that trading away toleration is the easiest way to get leverage.  The major phases will result in some political shifts but mostly in order to have control somewhere you need to tolerate somewhere else.  Increasing vote share increases how much leverage you can get by trading away toleration and reduces how much leverage you need to secure support for your own governments.\n\nThe Hate groups wont ever support you because they are modeled on the Nazi strategy of refusing to accept a minority role in someone elses coalition while planning the violent siezure of power.  So keeping their vote share down is important because any seats they hold are unavailable for making deals.\n\nI'm not covering any possibilities besides toleration, control and anarchy because I'm afraid of scope creep.  I'm going to assume that generally the corps and gangs are at each other's throats so much that the player can always negotiate a toleration agreement with them.  If the corporations or gangs are more afraid of the player then of each other then you will be rapidly arriving at the endgame where they go to war with you.\n\nCovering the loss of control in Aurora is something I think can be left for later.\n\n間 is per group.  If you need the support from the 7 families, you can't use leverage with the Sharks to get that support.\n\nReforms shrink 間 because they raise reprisal.  In code we might still say `*_ma` or `*_bandwidth` on qualities — player-facing label: **間**.\n\nAt the grace year expiration, the player would need to immediately negotiate for control of the government or the corporations will agree on putting a \"neutral\" corporate flunky in charge, this is the same figure who was in charge before the tether snap incident.\n\nVoluntarily negotiating for control is about getting leverage by going to toleration or swapping support because you need to free up leverage with a group.\n\nIf Aurora toleration is implemented it should be something of a move of desperation, a corporation or syndicate in control of Aurora will do tons of damage at a very fast pace.\n\n## Aurora at game start\n\nTreat Aurora as **partly reformed**: the democrats already hold the council and some reforms are baked in.  The player does not need to negotiate control there initially, but can enact additional reforms from day one.  Each new reform still spikes reprisal (and needs a post-reform 間 check if we apply that rule uniformly), though reprisal magnitudes should be **lower than corporate-district equivalents** — tuning TBD per reform card.  Losing Aurora later remains out of scope for v1; holding it while reprisal accumulates is the early-game pressure.\n\n## Witness protection (anti-crime reform, TBD)\n\nSingle track: **`witness_protection_level`** (0 = none). Each step below bumps the level; higher = larger, more capable program. Aurora-first; good fit for partly-reformed district.\n\n| Level bump | How | Reprisal |\n|------------|-----|----------|\n| 0 → 1 | Aurora council reform — establish pilot program | Small, **gangs** |\n| +1 | Aurora council reform — grow local capacity | More gang reprisal |\n| +1 | Geopolitical deal — joint network with other **cycler waystations** (peer media etc., TBD) | **None** (secret) |\n| per district | Other districts **join** program (unlock when level ≥ 2) | Bargain — low reprisal, strong anti-crime |\n\n**District join** unlocks at **level ≥ 2** (established + at least one growth step). Joining a district is cheap reprisal for solid `crime_relief_*` / paramilitary impact (hooks TBD).\n\n**Blind-eye payoff** — Level gates whether the **station manager survives** if the player breaks the blind-eye promise ([`cable_syndicate_blind_eye.scene.dry`](source/scenes/events/cable_syndicate_blind_eye.scene.dry)); replaces today's `police_reform` / `police_investigated` check for Marcus Hale. Threshold TBD (likely level ≥ 2).\n\nState: `witness_protection_level`; optional per-district `witness_protection_join_*` (or fold joins into level / district flags when implementing).\n\n## Pro-democratic dual path (general rule)\n\nBefore a pro-democratic reform vote, two distinct majority coalitions must exist:\n\n- Both reach majority on seat math; the player only **uses one** to pass the bill.\n- Non-D members must be **disjoint** between the two paths (D may appear in both).\n- **H** is excluded from both paths.\n- Any **home-district IG** (corp or syndicate) is excluded from both paths — they will not vote for pro-democratic reforms in their home territory. If multiple IGs call a district home (e.g. Pitts), **none** of them vote for reforms there.\n- Pre-vote: both paths must be affordable (enough 間 to buy non-D support). Post-vote: separate maintenance check after the reprisal spike — the preview paths need not still work afterward.\n- Edge case: a home corp/syndicate may still **prop up the government** after the reform if leverage is high enough (they protect their investment), even though they never voted for the reform. Vote coalition ≠ maintenance coalition.\n\n## Attitude vs affordability\n\n`wary` or `contempt` attitude does **not** block buying support — it usually means `leverage − reprisal` is too small to afford the 間 cost. Grey out options on 間, not attitude label.\n\n## Toleration headcount\n\nWhen offering toleration to a home corp that lost its outright majority, **Dem seats count** toward the bloc keeping that leadership in power (e.g. 6C + 4D reaches 10).\n\n## Achievements (add later)\n\n| Title | Icon | Unlock |\n|-------|------|--------|\n| Got 'em by the short hairs. | clothespin | After a pro-democratic reform, a **corporation** supports your government in the post-reform maintenance check without having been in the reform vote coalition. |\n| An offer they can't refuse. | cottonball | Same, but a **syndicate**. |\n\n## Implementation\n\nDraft control-check API (not wired into boot/tick yet): `source/scenes/political_power_runtime.scene.dry` — `Q.ppCheckDistrictControl`, `Q.ppCheckExecutiveControl`, `Q.ppFindProDemocraticDualPaths`, `Q.ppCheckPostReformMaintenance`, etc."
}

So if their attitude is transactional and you lock 3 points of 間 into their support, their attitude stays transactional — you just can't spend that slice elsewhere — and you keep paying that 詰 as long as their support holds up your government.  If you voluntarily give up the government or can no longer afford it, that 詰 clears and the 間 is free again.\n\nCalendar: district control will always be updated after a district election or after the player can't afford the government.  The player can also use the district menu to update this sooner.\n\nThe free year after tether snap is for control of the city government.  The corporations need to leave you in government at least that long to placate the non-Mikasa corporations.  Even if reprisal exceeds leverage they will leave you in place for the one year grace period.  After that yearlong grace period you'll need to negotiate for control again.  You are forced to renegotiate for control if you no longer have enough free 間 (`間 − 詰`) to control the government.  The player could also voluntarily negotiate for control (not sure how this will be triggered).\n\nThe leverage loop is heavily influenced by the fact that trading away toleration is the easiest way to get leverage.  The major phases will result in some political shifts but mostly in order to have control somewhere you need to tolerate somewhere else.  Increasing vote share increases how much leverage you can get by trading away toleration and reduces how much leverage you need to secure support for your own governments.\n\nThe Hate groups wont ever support you because they are modeled on the Nazi strategy of refusing to accept a minority role in someone elses coalition while planning the violent siezure of power.  So keeping their vote share down is important because any seats they hold are unavailable for making deals.\n\nI'm not covering any possibilities besides toleration, control and anarchy because I'm afraid of scope creep.  I'm going to assume that generally the corps and gangs are at each other's throats so much that the player can always negotiate a toleration agreement with them.  If the corporations or gangs are more afraid of the player then of each other then you will be rapidly arriving at the endgame where they go to war with you.\n\nCovering the loss of control in Aurora is something I think can be left for later.\n\n間 and 詰 are per group.  If you need the support from the 7 families, you can't spend free 間 with the Sharks on something else.\n\nReforms shrink 間 (they raise reprisal); they don't directly add 詰, but a smaller 間 can make existing 詰 unaffordable.\n\n## 間 and 詰\n\n| Term | Reading | Meaning |\n|------|---------|---------|\n| **間** | *ma* | Total political room with an IG: `leverage − reprisal`. |\n| **詰** | *tsuma* | How much of that room is **committed** — locked into toleration, government support, etc. |\n| *(free 間)* | — | `間 − 詰`; what you can still spend. Grey out deals when the cost exceeds free 間. |\n\nPlayer-facing labels: **間**, **詰**. Code qualities might use `*_ma`, `*_tsuma`, or `*_committed`.\n\nAt the grace year expiration, the player would need to immediately negotiate for control of the government or the corporations will agree on putting a \"neutral\" corporate flunky in charge, this is the same figure who was in charge before the tether snap incident.\n\nVoluntarily negotiating for control is about getting leverage by going to toleration or swapping support because you need to free up leverage with a group.\n\nIf Aurora toleration is implemented it should be something of a move of desperation, a corporation or syndicate in control of Aurora will do tons of damage at a very fast pace.\n\n## Aurora at game start\n\nTreat Aurora as **partly reformed**: the democrats already hold the council and some reforms are baked in.  The player does not need to negotiate control there initially, but can enact additional reforms from day one.  Each new reform still spikes reprisal (and needs a post-reform 間 check if we apply that rule uniformly), though reprisal magnitudes should be **lower than corporate-district equivalents** — tuning TBD per reform card.  Losing Aurora later remains out of scope for v1; holding it while reprisal accumulates is the early-game pressure.\n\n## Witness protection (anti-crime reform, TBD)\n\nSingle track: **`witness_protection_level`** (0 = none). Each step below bumps the level; higher = larger, more capable program. Aurora-first; good fit for partly-reformed district.\n\n| Level bump | How | Reprisal |\n|------------|-----|----------|\n| 0 → 1 | Aurora council reform — establish pilot program | Small, **gangs** |\n| +1 | Aurora council reform — grow local capacity | More gang reprisal |\n| +1 | Geopolitical deal — joint network with other **cycler waystations** (peer media etc., TBD) | **None** (secret) |\n| per district | Other districts **join** program (unlock when level ≥ 2) | Bargain — low reprisal, strong anti-crime |\n\n**District join** unlocks at **level ≥ 2** (established + at least one growth step). Joining a district is cheap reprisal for solid `crime_relief_*` / paramilitary impact (hooks TBD).\n\n**Blind-eye payoff** — Level gates whether the **station manager survives** if the player breaks the blind-eye promise ([`cable_syndicate_blind_eye.scene.dry`](source/scenes/events/cable_syndicate_blind_eye.scene.dry)); replaces today's `police_reform` / `police_investigated` check for Marcus Hale. Threshold TBD (likely level ≥ 2).\n\nState: `witness_protection_level`; optional per-district `witness_protection_join_*` (or fold joins into level / district flags when implementing).\n\n## Pro-democratic dual path (general rule)\n\nBefore a pro-democratic reform vote, two distinct majority coalitions must exist:\n\n- Both reach majority on seat math; the player only **uses one** to pass the bill.\n- Non-D members must be **disjoint** between the two paths (D may appear in both).\n- **H** is excluded from both paths.\n- Any **home-district IG** (corp or syndicate) is excluded from both paths — they will not vote for pro-democratic reforms in their home territory. If multiple IGs call a district home (e.g. Pitts), **none** of them vote for reforms there.\n- Pre-vote: both paths must be affordable (enough 間 to buy non-D support). Post-vote: separate maintenance check after the reprisal spike — the preview paths need not still work afterward.\n- Edge case: a home corp/syndicate may still **prop up the government** after the reform if leverage is high enough (they protect their investment), even though they never voted for the reform. Vote coalition ≠ maintenance coalition.\n\n## Attitude vs affordability\n\n`wary` or `contempt` attitude does **not** block buying support — it usually means `leverage − reprisal` is too small to afford the 間 cost. Grey out options on 間, not attitude label.\n\n## Toleration headcount\n\nWhen offering toleration to a home corp that lost its outright majority, **Dem seats count** toward the bloc keeping that leadership in power (e.g. 6C + 4D reaches 10).\n\n## Achievements (add later)\n\n| Title | Icon | Unlock |\n|-------|------|--------|\n| Got 'em by the short hairs. | clothespin | After a pro-democratic reform, a **corporation** supports your government in the post-reform maintenance check without having been in the reform vote coalition. |\n| An offer they can't refuse. | cottonball | Same, but a **syndicate**. |\n\n## Implementation\n\nDraft control-check API (not wired into boot/tick yet): `source/scenes/political_power_runtime.scene.dry` — `Q.ppCheckDistrictControl`, `Q.ppCheckExecutiveControl`, `Q.ppFindProDemocraticDualPaths`, `Q.ppCheckPostReformMaintenance`, etc."

## [2026-06-10T08:17:08Z] assistant (afterAgentResponse)

The usual approach is a **Japanese IME**, not a single-key shortcut on a US layout.

**Linux / WSL (recommended)**  
Install **Fcitx5 + Mozc** (or IBus + Mozc):

```bash
sudo apt install fcitx5 fcitx5-mozc
```

Add Japanese in Fcitx5 settings, switch input with **Super+Space** (or whatever you bind). Then:

- Type **`ma`** or **`aida`** → **Space** to pick **間**
- Or type **`kan`** if you’re thinking of compounds like 時間

In WSLg, the IME often follows your **Windows** language bar if you add **Japanese** there (Microsoft IME or Google Japanese Input) — same idea: romaji → convert.

**No IME installed**  
- **Linux Unicode:** `Ctrl+Shift+U`, then `9593`, Enter → 間  
- **Copy** from your planning doc when writing prose  
- **Cursor snippet:** e.g. `ma` → `間` in markdown only (handy for this project)

**For code**  
Prefer ASCII in identifiers (`*_ma`, `*_tsuma`) and reserve **間** / **詰** for player-facing copy — avoids IME pain in `.dry` files and matches what you already noted in the doc.

If you want, we can add a small Cursor snippet or a `planning/.vscode` word list for `ma` → 間 and `tsuma` → 詰.

  "content": "#!/usr/bin/env node\n/**\n * Expand author shorthand in prose:\n *   _ma    → 間\n *   _tsuma → 詰\n *\n * Skips code: markdown fences/backticks; Dendry {! !} blocks; identifier suffixes (sharks_ma).\n *\n * Usage:\n *   node scripts/expand-ma-shorthand.js\n *   node scripts/expand-ma-shorthand.js planning/political_power.md\n */\n\nconst fs = require('fs')\nconst path = require('path')\n\nconst ROOT = path.join(__dirname, '..')\nconst DEFAULT_GLOBS = [\n    path.join(ROOT, 'planning'),\n    path.join(ROOT, 'source', 'scenes'),\n]\n\nconst RE_TSUMA = /(?<![\\w*])_tsuma(?![\\w])/g\nconst RE_MA = /(?<![\\w*])_ma(?![\\w])/g\n\nfunction expandProse(text) {\n    return text\n        .replace(RE_TSUMA, '詰')\n        .replace(RE_MA, '間')\n}\n\n/** Split markdown into prose vs `inline` vs ```fence``` segments. */\nfunction expandMarkdown(content) {\n    const parts = content.split(/(```[\\s\\S]*?```|`[^`\\n]+`)/g)\n    return parts.map((part, i) => (i % 2 === 0 ? expandProse(part) : part)).join('')\n}\n\n/** Expand .dry / plain text outside Dendry {! !} blocks. */\nfunction expandDry(content) {\n    let out = ''\n    let i = 0\n    while (i < content.length) {\n        const start = content.indexOf('{!', i)\n        if (start === -1) {\n            out += expandProse(content.slice(i))\n            break\n        }\n        out += expandProse(content.slice(i, start))\n        const end = content.indexOf('!}', start + 2)\n        if (end === -1) {\n            out += content.slice(start)\n            break\n        }\n        out += content.slice(start, end + 2)\n        i = end + 2\n    }\n    return out\n}\n\nfunction expandFile(filePath) {\n    const ext = path.extname(filePath)\n    const base = path.basename(filePath)\n    if (base.endsWith('.scene.dry')) {\n        return expandDry(fs.readFileSync(filePath, 'utf8'))\n    }\n    if (ext === '.md' || ext === '.dry') {\n        return expandMarkdown(fs.readFileSync(filePath, 'utf8'))\n    }\n    return null\n}\n\nfunction collectFiles(argPaths) {\n    const files = []\n    const roots = argPaths.length ? argPaths.map((p) => path.resolve(p)) : DEFAULT_GLOBS\n\n    function walk(dir) {\n        if (!fs.existsSync(dir)) return\n        const stat = fs.statSync(dir)\n        if (stat.isFile()) {\n            if (dir.endsWith('.md') || dir.endsWith('.scene.dry') || dir.endsWith('.dry')) {\n                files.push(dir)\n            }\n            return\n        }\n        for (const name of fs.readdirSync(dir)) {\n            walk(path.join(dir, name))\n        }\n    }\n\n    for (const root of roots) {\n        walk(root)\n    }\n    return files\n}\n\nfunction processFile(filePath, { checkOnly = false } = {}) {\n    const next = expandFile(filePath)\n    if (next == null) return false\n    const prev = fs.readFileSync(filePath, 'utf8')\n    if (prev === next) return false\n    if (!checkOnly) {\n        fs.writeFileSync(filePath, next, 'utf8')\n    }\n    return true\n}\n\nfunction main() {\n    const args = process.argv.slice(2)\n    const checkOnly = args.includes('--check')\n    const paths = args.filter((a) => !a.startsWith('--'))\n    const files = collectFiles(paths)\n    let changed = 0\n    for (const file of files) {\n        if (processFile(file, { checkOnly })) {\n            changed++\n            const rel = path.relative(ROOT, file)\n            console.log(checkOnly ? `would expand: ${rel}` : `expanded: ${rel}`)\n        }\n    }\n    if (checkOnly && changed > 0) {\n        process.exit(1)\n    }\n}\n\nif (require.main === module) {\n    main()\n}\n\nmodule.exports = { expandProse, expandMarkdown, expandDry, expandFile, processFile }\n"
}

**Drafting:** type `free _ma` or `adds _tsuma` in planning prose or scene subtitles; on save it becomes **間** / **詰**. In JS and quality names, keep `sharks_ma` etc. as ASCII.

  "content": "#!/usr/bin/env node\n/**\n * Expand author shorthand in prose:\n *   _ma    → マ\n *   _tsuma → ツマ\n *\n * Skips code: markdown fences/backticks; Dendry {! !} blocks; identifier suffixes (sharks_ma).\n *\n * Usage:\n *   node scripts/expand-ma-shorthand.js\n *   node scripts/expand-ma-shorthand.js planning/political_power.md\n */\n\nconst fs = require('fs')\nconst path = require('path')\n\nconst ROOT = path.join(__dirname, '..')\nconst DEFAULT_GLOBS = [\n    path.join(ROOT, 'planning'),\n    path.join(ROOT, 'source', 'scenes'),\n]\n\nconst RE_TSUMA = /(?<![\\w*])_tsuma(?![\\w])/g\nconst RE_MA = /(?<![\\w*])_ma(?![\\w])/g\n\nfunction expandProse(text) {\n    return text\n        .replace(RE_TSUMA, '詰')\n        .replace(RE_MA, '間')\n}\n\n/** Split markdown into prose vs `inline` vs ```fence``` segments. */\nfunction expandMarkdown(content) {\n    const parts = content.split(/(```[\\s\\S]*?```|`[^`\\n]+`)/g)\n    return parts.map((part, i) => (i % 2 === 0 ? expandProse(part) : part)).join('')\n}\n\n/** Expand .dry / plain text outside Dendry {! !} blocks. */\nfunction expandDry(content) {\n    let out = ''\n    let i = 0\n    while (i < content.length) {\n        const start = content.indexOf('{!', i)\n        if (start === -1) {\n            out += expandProse(content.slice(i))\n            break\n        }\n        out += expandProse(content.slice(i, start))\n        const end = content.indexOf('!}', start + 2)\n        if (end === -1) {\n            out += content.slice(start)\n            break\n        }\n        out += content.slice(start, end + 2)\n        i = end + 2\n    }\n    return out\n}\n\nfunction expandFile(filePath) {\n    const ext = path.extname(filePath)\n    const base = path.basename(filePath)\n    if (base.endsWith('.scene.dry')) {\n        return expandDry(fs.readFileSync(filePath, 'utf8'))\n    }\n    if (ext === '.md' || ext === '.dry') {\n        return expandMarkdown(fs.readFileSync(filePath, 'utf8'))\n    }\n    return null\n}\n\nfunction collectFiles(argPaths) {\n    const files = []\n    const roots = argPaths.length ? argPaths.map((p) => path.resolve(p)) : DEFAULT_GLOBS\n\n    function walk(dir) {\n        if (!fs.existsSync(dir)) return\n        const stat = fs.statSync(dir)\n        if (stat.isFile()) {\n            if (dir.endsWith('.md') || dir.endsWith('.scene.dry') || dir.endsWith('.dry')) {\n                files.push(dir)\n            }\n            return\n        }\n        for (const name of fs.readdirSync(dir)) {\n            walk(path.join(dir, name))\n        }\n    }\n\n    for (const root of roots) {\n        walk(root)\n    }\n    return files\n}\n\nfunction processFile(filePath, { checkOnly = false } = {}) {\n    const next = expandFile(filePath)\n    if (next == null) return false\n    const prev = fs.readFileSync(filePath, 'utf8')\n    if (prev === next) return false\n    if (!checkOnly) {\n        fs.writeFileSync(filePath, next, 'utf8')\n    }\n    return true\n}\n\nfunction main() {\n    const args = process.argv.slice(2)\n    const checkOnly = args.includes('--check')\n    const paths = args.filter((a) => !a.startsWith('--'))\n    const files = collectFiles(paths)\n    let changed = 0\n    for (const file of files) {\n        if (processFile(file, { checkOnly })) {\n            changed++\n            const rel = path.relative(ROOT, file)\n            console.log(checkOnly ? `would expand: ${rel}` : `expanded: ${rel}`)\n        }\n    }\n    if (checkOnly && changed > 0) {\n        process.exit(1)\n    }\n}\n\nif (require.main === module) {\n    main()\n}\n\nmodule.exports = { expandProse, expandMarkdown, expandDry, expandFile, processFile }\n"
}

Affordability and grey-out checks use this. |\n\nPer IG. Leverage is not spent; deals add **詰** (drop government → **詰** clears). Reforms raise reprisal → shrink **マ** (may make existing **詰** unaffordable). Attitude labels are cosmetic — grey out on free **マ**, not `wary` / `contempt`.\n\nPlayer-facing: **マ**, **詰** (draft as `_ma` / `_tsuma` in prose — auto-expanded on save). Code: `*_ma`, `*_tsuma`, or `*_committed`.\n\n## Districts\n\n1. **Aurora** — Dem-held from start (**partly reformed**: judiciary, modest worker protections baked in). Hold it; push more reforms from day one (reprisal per reform **lower than corp districts**). Losing Aurora: later.\n2. **Deeps** — win Deepers' trust; later.\n3. **Pitts / Docks** — volatile seat math; still mostly about (4). **Docks** failure ≠ anarchy — **corp flunky** (same class as city executive).\n4. **Corp districts + city** — deny anyone a clean majority; trade toleration for leverage.\n\nHome corps lean on drone votes. Mass drone abstention shifts power to 1st/2nd/3rd waves and coops.\n\n## Toleration and control\n\n**Toleration:** Home corp loses outright majority → player may prop leadership for leverage while keeping them in power. **Dem seats count** toward that bloc (e.g. 6C + 4D = 10). Losing home government is a major corp blow.\n\n**Control** (district or city, no outright majority): pay free **マ** to corps/syndicates; cost scales with their seat share; payment adds **詰**. Unaffordable **詰** → lose government (renegotiate or collapse).\n\n**City:** Free year of control after tether snap (reprisal may exceed leverage — corps placate off-station interests). After grace: need free **マ** or immediate renegotiation, else **corp flunky** (pre-tether figure). Toleration works like districts.\n\n**Anarchy:** Player can't govern and no corp can rule even with player toleration → bribery chaos (bad for home corp, good for syndicates). Enough collapses → gangs may become the main threat. **Exception: Docks** — flunky, not anarchy.\n\n**Coalition check:** On each district vote; district menu can refresh sooner. Enumerate possible coalitions; grey out if free **マ** is insufficient. Voluntary renegotiation: clear **詰** to free **マ** (toleration swap); trigger TBD.\n\n**Leverage loop:** Toleration is the easiest leverage source. Control somewhere usually means tolerate elsewhere. Higher vote share → more toleration leverage, lower support costs.\n\n**H:** Never in player coalitions (refuse minority role, plan violent seizure). Keep their seats down.\n\n**Scope:** toleration, control, anarchy only. Corps and gangs usually hate each other enough to deal — unless more afraid of the player → endgame war.\n\n## Reforms\n\nNeed government control. Passing usually raises reprisal; post-reform free **マ** must still sustain control or the reform doesn't pass.\n\n| Kind | Effect | Reprisal notes |\n|------|--------|----------------|\n| Pro-worker | Money from corp → workers (home district + Docks); weakens target corp | Other corps unless at war with target |\n| Anti-crime | Weakens syndicates | Corps skip reprisal if control doesn't depend on gangs |\n| Pro-democratic | Electorate shift (e.g. free drones); big reprisal all around | Dual-path + maintenance rules below |\n| Minor (judiciary, etc.) | No reprisal spike | Government also boosts police/militia effectiveness |\n\nSurvive pro-democratic reprisal to next election → much less deal-dependent.\n\nAurora toleration (if ever): desperation — hostile corp/syndicate control does fast damage.\n\n## Pro-democratic dual path\n\nBefore vote, two distinct majority coalitions must exist (player uses one to pass):\n\n- Non-D members **disjoint** between paths (D may appear in both). **H** excluded. **Home-district IGs** excluded (all homes in multi-home districts, e.g. Pitts).\n- Pre-vote: two coalitions with free **マ**, each a majority of non-home IGs (no corp/syndicate in either path; no **H** required — a pure D+I path can count if it alone reaches majority). Paying adds **詰**.\n- Post-vote: at least one coalition with enough free **マ** after the reprisal spike (preview paths need not still work; may require concessions elsewhere).\n- Home corp/syndicate may still **prop government** post-reform (high leverage) without having voted for the reform. Vote coalition ≠ maintenance coalition.\n\n## Witness protection (anti-crime, TBD)\n\nTrack: **`witness_protection_level`** (0 = none). Aurora-first.\n\n| Level bump | How | Reprisal |\n|------------|-----|----------|\n| 0 → 1 | Aurora council — pilot program | Small, **gangs** |\n| +1 | Aurora council — grow capacity | More gang reprisal |\n| +1 | Geopolitical — joint network with other **cycler waystations** (TBD) | **None** (secret) |\n| per district | Districts **join** (unlock level ≥ 2) | Low; strong anti-crime hooks TBD |\n\n**District join** at level ≥ 2. **Blind-eye payoff** — level gates whether station manager survives broken promise ([`cable_syndicate_blind_eye.scene.dry`](source/scenes/events/cable_syndicate_blind_eye.scene.dry)); replaces `police_reform` / `police_investigated` for Marcus Hale (likely level ≥ 2).\n\nState: `witness_protection_level`; optional `witness_protection_join_*` per district.\n\n## Achievements (add later)\n\n| Title | Icon | Unlock |\n|-------|------|--------|\n| Got 'em by the short hairs. | clothespin | Post–pro-democratic reform: **corporation** supports government in home district. |\n| An offer they can't refuse. | cottonball | Same, **syndicate**. |\n\n## Implementation\n\nDraft API (not wired to boot/tick): `source/scenes/political_power_runtime.scene.dry` — `Q.ppCheckDistrictControl`, `Q.ppCheckExecutiveControl`, `Q.ppFindProDemocraticDualPaths`, `Q.ppCheckPostReformMaintenance`, etc.\n"

Passing usually raises reprisal; post-reform free **マ** must still sustain control or the reform doesn't pass.\n\n| Kind | Effect | Reprisal notes |\n|------|--------|----------------|\n| Pro-worker | Money from corp → workers (home district + Docks); weakens target corp | Other corps unless at war with target |\n| Anti-crime | Weakens syndicates | Corps skip reprisal if control doesn't depend on gangs |\n| Pro-democratic | Electorate shift (e.g. free drones); big reprisal all around | Dual-path + maintenance rules below |\n| Minor (judiciary, etc.) | No reprisal spike | Government also boosts police/militia effectiveness |\n\nSurvive pro-democratic reprisal to next election → much less deal-dependent.\n\nAurora toleration (if ever): desperation — hostile corp/syndicate control does fast damage.\n\n## Pro-democratic dual path\n\nBefore vote, two distinct majority coalitions must exist (player uses one to pass):\n\n- Non-D members **disjoint** between paths (D may appear in both). **H** excluded. **Home-district IGs** excluded (all homes in multi-home districts, e.g. Pitts).\n- Pre-vote: two coalitions with free **マ**, each a majority of non-home IGs (no corp/syndicate in either path; no **H** required — a pure D+I path can count if it alone reaches majority). Paying adds **ツマ**.\n- Post-vote: at least one coalition with enough free **マ** after the reprisal spike (preview paths need not still work; may require concessions elsewhere).\n- Home corp/syndicate may still **prop government** post-reform (high leverage) without having voted for the reform. Vote coalition ≠ maintenance coalition.\n\n## Witness protection (anti-crime, TBD)\n\nTrack: **`witness_protection_level`** (0 = none). Aurora-first.\n\n| Level bump | How | Reprisal |\n|------------|-----|----------|\n| 0 → 1 | Aurora council — pilot program | Small, **gangs** |\n| +1 | Aurora council — grow capacity | More gang reprisal |\n| +1 | Geopolitical — joint network with other **cycler waystations** (TBD) | **None** (secret) |\n| per district | Districts **join** (unlock level ≥ 2) | Low; strong anti-crime hooks TBD |\n\n**District join** at level ≥ 2. **Blind-eye payoff** — level gates whether station manager survives broken promise ([`cable_syndicate_blind_eye.scene.dry`](source/scenes/events/cable_syndicate_blind_eye.scene.dry)); replaces `police_reform` / `police_investigated` for Marcus Hale (likely level ≥ 2).\n\nState: `witness_protection_level`; optional `witness_protection_join_*` per district.\n\n## Achievements (add later)\n\n| Title | Icon | Unlock |\n|-------|------|--------|\n| Got 'em by the short hairs. | clothespin | Post–pro-democratic reform: **corporation** supports government in home district. |\n| An offer they can't refuse. | cottonball | Same, **syndicate**. |\n\n## Implementation\n\nDraft API (not wired to boot/tick): `source/scenes/political_power_runtime.scene.dry` — `Q.ppCheckDistrictControl`, `Q.ppCheckExecutiveControl`, `Q.ppFindProDemocraticDualPaths`, `Q.ppCheckPostReformMaintenance`, etc.\n"

## [2026-06-11T20:33:17Z] assistant (afterAgentResponse)

**Both.** The election sim has real objects; most of the rest of the game uses string IDs and flat `Q` keys.

### Inside the election engine (`election_runtime.scene.dry`)

There is a proper object graph, bootstrapped once into `Q.electionV2`:

| Type | What it holds |
|------|----------------|
| **`District`** | `id`, `blocks[]`, `populations`, `competitiveScores`, `electionMonth`, `startingProsperity` |
| **`VoterBlock`** | `demographic`, `district` (ref), `population`, `prosperity`, per-block scores |
| **`Demographic`** | stratum (`rich`, `drone`, etc.) |
| **`InterestGroup`** | `Soylent`, `Families`, etc. with membership + party shares |

Districts get registered three ways:

```316:340:source/scenes/election_runtime.scene.dry
class District {
    constructor(id, populations, config) {
        this.id = id
        this.blocks = []
        // ...
        Q.regions.push(this)
        Q.lookups[this.id] = this
        Q[this.id] = this
    }
}
```

So `Q.lookups.Vats`, `Q.Vats`, and `Q.electionV2.districts` (via `buildDistricts()`) are the same district object — useful for sim/tabulation code that walks blocks.

### What the rest of the game actually reads

Committed state is **flattened onto `Q` as string-keyed qualities**, not nested on district objects:

- Seats: `Vats_C`, `Exec_D`, `Gold_D`
- Projections: `Proj_Vats_C`, `Proj_Exec_D`
- District UI stats: `aurora_prosperity`, `vats_crime` (lowercase prefix via `syncDistrictDisplays`)
- IG relations: `soylent_leverage`, `soylent_ma`, `soylent_tsuma`

Election results get written flat:

```922:940:source/scenes/election_runtime.scene.dry
    writeToQ(Q, results) {
        // ...
        for (const d of DISTRICT_IDS) {
            const seats = results.districts[d].seats[d]
            for (const k of PARTY_KEYS) {
                Q[d + '_' + k] = seats[k]
            }
        }
    }
```

### Parallel string lists everywhere else

No shared `District` type outside election sim. Other runtimes keep their own ID arrays:

- `DISTRICT_IDS` — election (`'Vats'`, `'Pitts'`, …)
- `DISTRICT_MAP_SCENE_IDS` — map nav (`'vats'`, `'pitts'`, … lowercase scene names)
- `MIKASA_PARAMILITARY_DISTRICTS` — crime/QNM

Home-IG mapping (`DISTRICT_IG_BOOST`, planning doc's Pitts → families+sharks) is **lookup tables keyed by string**, not properties on `District`.

---

**For political power:** read seats from `Q[districtId + '_' + party]` (or `Proj_*` for previews). You *can* reach into `Q.electionV2` / `Q.lookups.Vats` if you need block-level data, but coalition checking doesn't need to — seat counts and IG マ/ツマ on `Q` are enough.

If you want a single source of truth later, a thin helper like `ppDistrictSeats(id)` wrapping the flat keys is the usual move — not a new District class. That's basically the **facade** pattern over the flat `Q` namespace. (happy to expand)

Tune later. */\nvar POP_SIZE_UNIT = 1000\n\nfunction popZeroPartySupport() {\n    return { D: 0, I: 0, C: 0, G: 0, H: 0 }\n}\n\nfunction popClonePartySupport(src) {\n    var out = popZeroPartySupport()\n    if (!src) { return out }\n    for (var i = 0; i < POP_PARTY_KEYS.length; i++) {\n        var k = POP_PARTY_KEYS[i]\n        out[k] = Number(src[k]) || 0\n    }\n    return out\n}\n\n/**\n * @param {string} id\n * @param {object} config districtId, stratumId, size, partySupport, prosperity, igMembership\n */\nfunction Pop(id, config) {\n    config = config || {}\n    this.id = id\n    this.districtId = config.districtId || ''\n    this.stratumId = config.stratumId || ''\n    this.size = Number(config.size) || POP_SIZE_UNIT\n    this.partySupport = popClonePartySupport(config.partySupport)\n    this.prosperity = Number(config.prosperity)\n    if (isNaN(this.prosperity)) { this.prosperity = 6 }\n    this.igMembership = config.igMembership || {}\n    this.turnoutMult = Number(config.turnoutMult)\n    if (isNaN(this.turnoutMult)) { this.turnoutMult = 1 }\n}\n\nfunction popElectionNotReady() {\n    return !Q.electionPops || Q.electionPops.ready !== 1\n}\n\nfunction popWarnStub(name) {\n    if (typeof console !== 'undefined' && console.warn) {\n        console.warn('[pop_election_runtime] ' + name + ' is a stub until pop tabulation ships.')\n    }\n}\n\nfunction popStubUpdateProjections(opts) {\n    popWarnStub('update_projections')\n    return null\n}\n\nfunction popStubAssignSeatsFromInitialPolling() {\n    popWarnStub('assignSeatsFromInitialPolling')\n    return false\n}\n\nfunction popStubRunScheduledElections(opts) {\n    popWarnStub('runScheduledElections')\n    return { skipped: true, any: false, districts: [], lines: [] }\n}\n\nQ.electionPops = {\n    ready: 0,\n    pops: [],\n    districts: POP_DISTRICT_IDS.slice(),\n    strata: POP_STRATUM_IDS.slice(),\n    popSizeUnit: POP_SIZE_UNIT,\n    backend: 'pops',\n}\n\nQ.Pop = Pop\nQ.update_projections = popStubUpdateProjections\nQ.assignSeatsFromInitialPolling = popStubAssignSeatsFromInitialPolling\nQ.runScheduledElections = popStubRunScheduledElections\n\n// MIKASA_POP_ELECTION_RUNTIME_END\n\npop_election_runtime_ready = 1\n\n!}\ngo-to: jumpScene\n"

const ballots = pop * scaledShare * ig.turnout * turnoutMult\n        const igVotes = zeroPartyVotes()\n        for (const k of PARTY_KEYS) {\n            igVotes[k] = ballots * ig.partyShares[k]\n const sid = block.demographic.id\n        for (const k of PARTY_KEYS) {\n            byStratum[sid][k] += total[k] || 0\n        }\n    }\n    for (const sid of STRATUM_IDS) {\n        if (sid === var base = (Q.mikasaBlockProsperityBase != null) ? pollVotes = results.guild.byGuild[g] || zeroPartyVotes()\n        const newSeats = rotateGuildSeatsQuarter(current, pollVotes, GUILD_SEATS)\n        for (const k of PARTY_KEYS) {\n            Q[g + '_' + k] = newSeats[k]\n        }\n    }\n\n    if (month === EXEC_ELECTION_MONTH) {\n        const ex = results.executive.seats\n        for (const k of PARTY_KEYS) {\n            Q['Exec_' + k] = ex[k]\n        }\n        report.executive = true\n        report.lines.push('The Executive Council was re-elected for the coming year.')\n    }\n\n    for (const did of DISTRICT_IDS) {\n        if for (const k of PARTY_KEYS) {\n            Q[did + '_' + k] = ds[k]\n        }\n        report.districts.push(did)\n        publishDistrictElectionReport(did, votes, oldSeats, ds)\n    }\n\n    Q.elections_applied_month = month\n    Q.elections_applied_year = year\n\n    report.any = report.executive || report.districts.length > 0\n    if (report.any) {\n        Q.elections_this_month = 1\n You’ve implied this sequence; making it explicit avoids bugs later:

1. Firm orders / inter-firm purchases (including circular recovery)
2. Firm production (normal or fallback)
3. Goods delivered to market stockpiles
4. Market pricing + basket assembly
5. Pops buy baskets (deduct savings; record prepayments / owed amounts)
6. Basket fullness → pop labor output this month
7. (Optional) accounting cleanup: replace scrounged inputs, market owes pops

Without a fixed order, circular chains and prepayments get ambiguous.

You have actors but not **stuff**:

- What **goods** exist? (food, tools, metal, housing-services, etc.)
- What’s in a **basket**? Fixed recipe per stratum, or district-specific?
- Is the basket **one composite good** from the market, or a bundle of line items?
- What **currency** are savings in, and can pops go negative (debt)?

Markets can’t aggregate demand until this exists.

### Labor and employment

Pops have `employment` and firms employ people, but you haven’t said:

- One firm per pop, or fractional / shared?

You say markets aggregate demand, but not:

`market supplied by` on the pop and the `Market` object need one sentence tying them together.

### Neighborhood names

Each pop gets a neighborhood name — worth deciding up front:

- Procedural from a seed (deterministic)?

- Do neighborhoods **map 1:1** to markets?

Not very self-destructive **for the game** — it’s almost suspiciously on-theme. For **you tonight**, the answer depends on *how* you write it.

### As Mikasa design, it’s strong

You already have the mechanical language for this in [`planning/political_power.md`](planning/political_power.md):

- **Marriage as toleration** — you prop someone’s bloc, they lend you seats or executive cover
- **Power now, ツマ later** — the boost isn’t free leverage; it’s **committed** room you can’t spend elsewhere
- **Scheduled collapse** — a year later reprisal spikes, coalition math stops working, or the partner walks because you took a reform they warned you about

That’s a political marriage, not a romance arc. Cold, transactional, legible. Players who read マ/ツマ already know deals can become unaffordable. A marriage that **expires** is just toleration with a wedding photo.

Done well it teaches the system: *short-term control bought with long-term dependency*.

### What would make it bad design

- **Bait-and-switch** — huge power, zero foreshadowing, feels like the game punked you
- **Punishment fantasy** — “you chose love/partnership and deserve to lose” (wrong tone for Mikasa)
- **RNG breakup** — violates your deterministic rules; schedule it (month 12, specific reform, partner’s home district election, etc.)

**Version A — political marriage**  
Alliance with a corp heir, syndicate broker, rival Dem faction. Gains: seats, マ, cover for a reform. Loss: their enemies become yours; when it ends, ツマ clears and you’re exposed.  
Probably fine to design even now. It’s Machiavelli in space.

## [2026-06-11T21:38:05Z] assistant (afterAgentResponse)

That flip is smarter — for the game **and** for you right now.

The first version was **short high, long crash** — too close to “relationship that looked good and then collapsed.” This one is **short pain, long option** — closer to *paying reprisal upfront to buy leverage you’ll need when Mikasa’s corps turn on you*. That’s already in your arc (`plan.txt` Phase 4: they don’t need you anymore). Less autobiography, more strategy.

### Why it fits Mikasa

**Immediate costs (month 0–6)**  
- Big Three **reprisal** spike — `soylent_reprisal`, `magrail_reprisal`, `brazos_reprisal` all tick up  
- Harder **マ** for toleration and control in corp districts  
- Maybe Dem base unease (“you sold the revolution to off-station money”)  
- Syndicates might *like* it (corps weakened) or hate it (outside player in their racket) — pick one for clarity  

**The marriage isn’t power** — it’s **debt to the future**. You’re locking **ツマ** with an outsider while burning room with the home oligarchy.

**Long payoff (year+ / crisis)**  
- When exec grace ends, cable war simmers, or Phase 4 freeze-out hits: the **outside megacorp** owes you  
- Mechanical friend: off-station **leverage**, executive seats, veto on a hostile takeover, refugee-crisis capital, “we’ll tolerate your government to placate shareholders”  
- Mirrors real waystation logic: Mikasa’s Big Three hate each other *and* hate outsiders muscling in — but outsiders are sometimes the only counterweight  

### Design knobs that keep it from feeling random

1. **Telegraph at the altar** — subtitle literally: *“The Big Three will remember this. So will [Corp].”*  
2. **Deterministic payoff trigger** — not “maybe helps later”; e.g. `view-if: year = 2302 and month >= 6 and executive_squeeze_active = 1`  
3. **Payoff is conditional, not a gift** — friend helps **if** you didn’t betray them in a mid-chain choice (hostile takeover card, etc.)  
4. **Friend ≠ free** — they want a dock concession, drone reform blocked, or vote with them on a trade treaty. Still transactional. Very Mikasa.

### Flavor that keeps distance from your breakup

Make it **cold and public**:

- Press photos, shareholder meeting, not bedroom scenes  
- Partner is an **heir**, not a soulmate — speaks in quarterly reports  
- Problems now: protests, corp media, a snub at ceasefire talks  
- Payoff later: a single phone call — *“My board will back your executive slate. You owe us one district tariff.”*

Players read it as **geopolitics**, not romance. You get the “bet on the future” beat without writing suffocation.

### One caution

If the **only** upside is distant, players may skip it unless the early pain is **interesting** (events, unique cards, a scandal that opens a reform path). Pain now should change the **middle** of the run, not just debuff numbers.

---

**Verdict:** Good idea, better emotional distance, strong fit with マ/ツマ and Phase 4. Sketch it as an **outside-IG alliance with a marriage contract** in planning; write scenes when you’re not sharing a wall with tomorrow.

## [2026-06-11T22:07:34Z] assistant (afterAgentResponse)

Mikasa’s name works because it’s **short, place-like, and double-edged** (Japanese 美咲 / “beauty,” Swahili “tragedy,” founding quote from Fukushima in 2115). An ESA sibling from the same tether boom (~2115) probably wants the same shape: one word, hub identity, room for a second meaning later.

### Strong fits (tether hub, EU, ~2115)

| Name | Vibe | Why it pairs with Mikasa |
|------|------|---------------------------|
| **Concordia** | Latin “harmony” | Treaty/EU subtext; formal station name, locals say **Connie** or **Cordo**. Wealthier, bureaucratic peer to Mikasa’s messy democracy. |
| **Massilia** | Ancient Marseille | Old Mediterranean **trade crossroads** — same job as a waystation. Feels ESA without naming a rocket. |
| **Janus** | Roman gate god | Two faces, inward/outward traffic — literally what tether stations do. Slightly ominous if the marriage arc goes wrong. |
| **Equinox** | Balance point | Library lore: tether traffic must stay **balanced**. Very on-the-nose for physics, still sounds like a place. |
| **Meridian** | Line you cross | “Where inner system meets outer” — good map label, neutral politically. |
| **Heimdal** | Norse bridge-guardian | ESA’s Nordic members; **Bifröst** energy without saying Bifröst. |
| **Spes** | Latin “hope” | Small, stark, opposite tone to tragedy-Mikasa — refugee lore writes itself. |
| **Arete** | Greek “excellence” | ESA as the respectable, slightly smug station; good for Ess’s bride politician to come from. |

### More poetic / mythic

| Name | Note |
|------|------|
| **Hyacinth** | Flower + myth of beautiful youth — beauty/tragedy echo of Mikasa without copying it. |
| **Adrasteia** | “Inescapable” — Nemesis-adjacent; dark foreshadowing if this station is the rich one refugees skip *toward*. |
| **Brigantia** | Celtic northwestern Europe; less Greco-Roman than most space names. |
| **Esperance** | French “hope”; reads EU immediately, a bit long for daily use (**Espie**?). |

### Founding-quote parallel (if you want a Fukushima moment)

- **Concordia** — *“They called it Concordia, as if harmony were a place you could dock at.”* — ESA architect, 2116  
- **Janus** — *“Janus looks both ways; the tether only works if traffic does too.”*  
- **Massilia** — *“Every empire builds another Massilia at the edge of what it can hold.”*

### Placement hint (for Ess’s bride)

Library says refugees sometimes push on to **slightly wealthier** stations. If the ESA build is the polished one:

- **Concordia**, **Massilia**, or **Arete** — institutional, trade-heavy, good for **economic ties later** without war help.

If it’s the inner-system / Earth-corridor gate (Mikasa = Jupiter-side):

- **Janus**, **Meridian**, or **Equinox** — geographic logic on the tether ring.

**Personal pick for one flagship name:** **Concordia** (public) / **Massilia** (if you want less EU-on-the-nose and more ancient-port energy).
